title: Le Maître chat ou le Chat botté - Puss in Boots / Master Cat

keywords: le maître chat ou le chat botté - puss in boots / master cat
full_text:
An honest miller died, leaving behind nothing in this world to his three sons except his watermill, his donkey, and his tomcat. The division of property was swift: the eldest son took the mill, the second took the donkey, while the youngest was left with only the cat.

The poor young man sat on a milestone, wringing his hands in despair. 'My brothers can join their trades together and earn an honest living,' he lamented, 'but as for me, when I have cooked this cat and made a fur muff of his skin, I must die of starvation on the highway.'

The cat, who was washing his whiskers in the grass, heard every word. Sitting upright on his hind paws, he looked at his master with shrewd, luminous eyes and said: 'Do not grieve, my good master. Only provide me with a sturdy canvas sack with running cords, and have a shoemaker craft me a pair of polished leather boots so that I may walk without slipping through brambles and briars, and you shall soon discover that your inheritance is far more valuable than you imagine.'

Though astonished to hear a cat speak, the miller's son remembered how cleverly the feline had hunted rats by feigning death in the flour bins. With his last few silver coins, he purchased the leather boots and the bag.

Puss buckled the boots onto his paws, slung the corded bag across his shoulders, and trotted into a nearby warren where young, plump wild rabbits fed upon fresh clover. He filled the sack with bran and tender parsley, laid the bag open on the ground, and stretched himself out like a dead carcass, holding the cords between his claws. Presently, a foolish young rabbit hopped into the sack to feast. Puss pulled the strings tight, bagged the prize, and set off with pride for the royal palace.

Arriving at the throne room, Puss bowed to the ground before the King. 'Sire,' he purred with courtly elegance, 'I present you with this wild rabbit from the estates of my noble master, the Marquis of Carabas, who has commanded me to lay this humble gift at your feet.'

'Tell your master,' the King replied, pleased by the fine game, 'that I thank him heartily and receive his gift with pleasure.'

A few days later, Puss concealed himself in a wheat field with his open sack and captured two plump partridges. He carried them to the King as a gift from the Marquis of Carabas, receiving another purse of silver and royal gratitude. For three months, the booted cat regularly carried gifts of game to the court, making the name of the Marquis of Carabas renowned for wealth and generosity.

One day, Puss learned that the King was to ride in his golden carriage along the banks of the river with his daughter, the most beautiful princess in the world. Rushing to his master, Puss ordered: 'Strip off your ragged clothes and jump into the river to bathe where I direct you, and leave the rest of your fortune in my paws!'

The miller's son obeyed without question. As the royal carriage approached, Puss leaped onto the road, wailing at the top of his lungs: 'Help! Help! The Marquis of Carabas is drowning! Save my lord!'

The King put his head out of the carriage window and recognized the booted cat who had brought him so many partridges. He immediately ordered his royal guards to plunge into the river and rescue the young man. While the drenched youth was pulled to safety, Puss approached the King and whispered that while his master was swimming, rogue thieves had stolen his magnificent garments (having concealed the old clothes under a large flat rock).

The King instantly commanded the grand master of the wardrobe to bring one of his own finest embroidered suits of velvet and satin. Dressed in royal attire, the miller's son appeared so handsome, tall, and noble that the princess fell deeply in love with him at first sight, and the King invited him to ride inside the royal coach.

Overjoyed, Puss ran ahead along the road. Coming upon peasants mowing grass in a lush meadow, he hissed fiercely: 'Good people! If you do not tell the King when he passes that this meadow belongs to the Marquis of Carabas, you shall all be chopped into mincemeat!' When the King stopped his carriage and asked whose meadow it was, the terrified mowers answered in unison: 'It belongs to my Lord Marquis of Carabas!' The King was astounded by his guest's vast landholdings.

Puss ran ahead and threatened reapers cutting a golden wheat field, who likewise told the King that the harvest belonged to the Marquis of Carabas. At last, Puss arrived at a magnificent castle of stone and marble belonging to a ferocious, immensely wealthy ogre, who owned all the surrounding lands and could transform himself into any beast at will.

Puss knocked boldly and asked for an audience. Bowing low, Puss said: 'I have heard it reported, noble lord, that you possess the supernatural power to transform yourself into any beast—such as a lion or an elephant.'

'It is true!' roared the ogre, and in a flash, he changed into a terrifying lion with a thunderous roar. Puss was so frightened that he scrambled up the tapestries to the gutters, nearly slipping on his leather boots.

When the ogre resumed his human form, laughing heartily, Puss climbed down, panting. 'That was marvelous!' said the cat. 'Yet surely it is completely impossible for a lord of your mighty stature to change into a creature as tiny as a rat or a mouse?'

'Impossible?' sneered the vain ogre. 'Watch this!'

In an instant, the ogre shrank into a tiny brown mouse that scurried across the floor. Puss leaped like lightning, pounced upon the mouse, and swallowed him in a single gulp!

Hearing the rumbling of the royal coach crossing the drawbridge, Puss ran to the gate, bowed low, and proclaimed: 'Welcome, Your Majesty, to the chateau of my Lord Marquis of Carabas!'

The King was dazzled by the castle's grandeur. A lavish feast, which the ogre had prepared for his friends, was served in the banquet hall. Delighted by the young man's nobility, modesty, and vast wealth, the King declared: 'It depends only on yourself, Lord Marquis, whether you shall become my son-in-law.'

The miller's son accepted with heartfelt gratitude, and that very evening, he married the beautiful princess. As for Puss, he was made a great lord of the realm, and from that day forward, he never chased mice again, except as an amusing recreation.
moral: Ingenuity, tact, and enterprise are often worth more than an inherited fortune.
